speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: The short-term impact of Brexit is mainly on the financial markets, more than on economies.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: The immediate impact of Brexit on currencies and stock markets has also not been a major concern for us.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Following the Brexit vote, as Members know, the British pound has declined sharply in value, and the US dollar and the yen have strengthened in global markets.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Other Asian currencies, including the Singapore dollar, also weakened against the US dollar, as is typical when there is a sudden increase in risks in global markets.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: The resulting movement of the Singapore dollar on a trade-weighted basis has been orderly and contained.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Stock markets also fell immediately after the Referendum, but have since recovered.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: We can expect repeated bouts of volatility in financial markets as Brexit is debated and negotiated.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: The first uncertainty has to do with what Brexit actually means.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: There is no clarity within the UK, even among proponents of Brexit, on the nature of its future relationship with the EU.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: This state of affairs may persist for some time.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: It is also not clear when the UK will formally trigger Page: 37 Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty, which serves formal notice to leave the EU.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Second, even after formal notice is served, negotiations between the UK and the EU are likely to be complex and prolonged.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: The basic conundrum is that the UK wants free access to the EU market but control over immigration from the EU, whereas the EU sees free access to its market and free movement of people as one package.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Both the UK and EU leaders will be mindful of their domestic political circumstances, and the EU will want to ensure that more member states are not encouraged to follow the UK.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: In short, there is no precedent for Brexit and no one can say how and when events will unfold.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Until the future trade and investment relationships between the UK and the EU are formally settled, the uncertainties will likely reduce investments and economic growth in the UK and, to some extent, in Europe as well.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: They will present another headwind in a generally subdued global economic outlook for the next few years.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: What happens over the longer term following Brexit is even less predictable and a deeper concern.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Analysts have begun to paint the possible scenarios.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: In the more optimistic scenarios, the UK and the EU arrive at a new and mutually beneficial arrangement for trade, investment and immigration.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: If, as a result, the UK retains substantial access to the EU single market, we should not underestimate its ability to regain economic competitiveness and strength and to remain a valuable economic partner for us in Singapore over the long term.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: However, a more pessimistic state of affairs cannot be ruled out.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: The key unpredictability is in the political dynamics, both within the UK and in Europe.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: If the UK is unable to hold itself together as a union, or if nationalism gathers pace among the EU's member countries, there will very likely be a permanent weakening in their economies.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: More divisive politics in the UK and the EU will also weaken the resolve to undertake needed economic and financial reforms for the long term.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Last week, the World Bank released a report stating that the Brexit Referendum outcome has marked a "historical shift in trade policy attitudes" that could impair global economic growth.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: If we do, indeed, see a shift towards protectionist policies worldwide, it will have major implications for Singapore, which thrives on an open global trading system.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: We must watch the developments carefully and be prepared to adjust our strategies so that we stay competitive as an economy and can retain good jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: GIC and Temasek, like other major global investors, can never be insulated from volatility in the financial markets.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: However, both GIC and Temasek make investment decisions for the long term and look beyond the short-term market booms and busts.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Their focus with regard to Brexit, for example, is to assess how it could fundamentally alter the long-term prospects for the EU and UK economies.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: From time to time, GIC and Temasek will face market dislocations.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: They aim to weather the ups and downs of the market and adopt investment strategies that can deliver good long-term Page: 38 returns.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: The 2008 Global Financial Crisis was a major case in point.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Global capital markets saw much larger declines than what we saw recently with the Brexit vote.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: MSCI World (Equities) fell by more than 40% from its peak to the trough during the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: The value of GIC and Temasek's investment portfolios declined significantly, together with the markets.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: But their portfolios recovered their value within one to two years and have continued to grow since then.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: We must expect a period of economic uncertainty over the next few years at least.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: What is especially critical is how politics will unfold in the UK and Europe.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am aware that Temasek Holdings has about 8% of its portfolio in Europe.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If you look at the actual numbers, we have large stakes in British Pounds like in Stan Chart, some in Lloyds, as well as in properties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How would that impact, because, as the Deputy Prime Minister has shared earlier, it might be prolonged, coupled with the fact that we have about 70% of our investments in both Asia and Singapore by Temasek Holdings and China has recalibrated itself the past year and the next couple of years?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Bearing in mind also that, like last year, our Budget, moving ahead, would be highly dependent on Temasek's Net Investment Returns (NIRs).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Will that, in a way, require us, as we prepare for Budget 2017 and beyond, to relook at our strategies and how we position ourselves and balance our books?

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: You have to remember that the NIR Framework is really a framework of looking at the returns over the next 20 years, which is a reasonably long period, and applying that then to the asset base in order to derive how much money can be spent in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: So, I would say we should not rush to a conclusion on the long-term implications of Brexit.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: For that matter, as far as Temasek and GIC are concerned, they have reasonably well-diversified portfolios.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Temasek has a more concentrated portfolio in Asia and it is also more concentrated in equities.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Even for Temasek, if you look at its equity portfolio, it is quite well-diversified across industry sectors.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: So, at any one point in time, you are hit by one cycle or another, but it is the overall portfolio over the long term that determines if you are fulfilling your mission of delivering good long-term value.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, can I ask whether MOF will work with the rest of the Government agencies like MOM to ensure that we do not allow these foreigners to adversely affect employment opportunities for Singaporeans in the FIs?

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Our framework for admitting talent to Singapore remains unchanged.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: They must be talented, they must be experienced and they must be able to prove their worth.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: MOM's framework looks, as Members know, at a few criteria: how much they are paid, and Page: 39 not just how much they are paid at any age, it actually varies by age.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: So, if you are someone in your mid-40s, if you are talented and experienced, it will be reflected in your pay.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: So, it is not a framework where anyone who wants to come, comes into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: But we have got to make sure that the framework does allow talented and experienced people – people with a track record that can add to teams in Singapore – to come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: It is what our firms need and what our economy needs.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: So, I would not worry too much about the perturbances in Europe leading to a sudden flood of the unwashed to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, may I ask him whether this trend will further dampen Singapore's export and, if it is so, will that affect Singapore's economy?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: And should MAS mitigate this currency trend in the future?

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: First, we have to always, when we think of currency in the Singapore context, distinguish between the bilateral currency movements and the movements of the Singapore dollar against the trade-weighted basket.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: Bilaterally, it is true that we have strengthened very significantly against the British pound.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: That is because the pound has collapsed in global markets.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: But if you look at the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies, it has not moved very much.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: In fact, it has depreciated slightly because the US dollar and Japanese yen have strengthened in global markets.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: So, essentially, this is typical of any instance that happens in the global markets, where you find that the bilateral rates move quite significantly, but, on balance, when you look at the Singapore dollar across the whole basket of currencies, it moves in a fairly moderate fashion.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: In this instance, the movement has been quite contained.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: There can be no precise answer to both questions.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: First, I think this is a complication in the ratification of the Free Trade Agreement with the EU.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: It does not rule out early ratification but we know the distractions that are taking place in Europe.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: We are pushing them, we are in constant touch with them, both diplomatically as well as amongst our trade officials.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: But this is a bit of a setback.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: With the UK, I think we should always remain open to a free trade agreement.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: I do not want to prejudge obviously what happens between the UK and Europe.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: If the UK does go ahead with its exit from the single market and decides to have a free trade agreement with Europe, it will be, of course, very keen to also have free trade agreements with other third parties like ourselves.

speaker: Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam
text: It is something which we are in constant touch with the British on.
